children: Live cattle futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange rose on Monday for a fourth consecutive session, after a monthly government report showed a bigger year-on-year drop in the number of cattle in US feedlots than analysts had expected, traders said.
After the market closed Friday, the USDA reported the number of cattle on feed as of November 1 at 99% of a year ago. Analysts surveyed by Reuters on average had expected a smaller decline, to 99.7%.
"It was a pretty wide miss, and the fourth miss in a row in this report from the market's perspective," said Brodrick Schmidt, a commodity broker and market analyst at U.S. Commodities LLC.

The USDA reported cattle placements into US feedlots during October at 93% of a year ago, below the average analyst estimate of 97%. Marketings during October were 95% of a year ago, near the average analyst estimate of 94.9%.
The report told traders that the US is not rebuilding its cattle herd at a brisk pace, Schmidt said, and "that prices will stay strong as long as consumer demand for beef stays strong."

Cash cattle markets have seen steady trade and prices firming, with cattle trades reaching $222 per hundredweight, cwt, last week and prices in the north up $7 per cwt, market analysts said.
The wholesale choice boxed beef cutout value rose $3.35 to $356.19 per hundredweight on Monday morning, the USDA said.
Meanwhile, CME lean hog futures closed mostly lower, pressured by sagging cash hog prices and weak demand for pork.

December lean hog futures (LHZ26) settled 0.150 cent lower at 52.450 cents per pound while most-active February hogs (LHG27) dipped to a fresh contract low during the session, before ending up 0.300 cent at 57.275 cents a pound. Four other lean hog contracts also set fresh lows in Monday's trade.
